title: Indica vs Sativa vs Hybrid
seoTitle: Indica vs Sativa vs Hybrid Explained | Uforia Dispensary
description: Indica, sativa and hybrid are familiar cannabis labels. Learn where the terms came from, why chemistry matters more and how to use them as a loose guide.
lede: Indica, sativa and hybrid are some of the first words people learn about cannabis. They can be a handy starting point, as long as you know where they came from and what they can and cannot tell you.

sections.heading: Where the labels came from
sections.html:
The names are botanical, and they are old. In 1753, the Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus described Cannabis sativa, based largely on hemp familiar in Europe. In 1785, the French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck described Cannabis indica, from plants collected in India that were noted for their intoxicating effects. Sativa comes from the Latin for "cultivated," and indica simply means "of India."

Since then, the way the words are used has drifted a long way from those first descriptions. Today, growers often use them for a plant's shape: indica-leaning plants tend to be short and bushy with broad leaflets, while sativa-leaning plants tend to be taller with narrow leaflets and a longer growing season. A hybrid mixes traits of both.

sections.heading: What the labels have come to mean
sections.html:
In dispensaries, the words have taken on a second meaning. "Indica" is often used for strains people associate with relaxed, body-centered experiences, "sativa" for those people describe as uplifting or energizing, and "hybrid" for everything in between.

The catch is that decades of crossbreeding have blended these lines so thoroughly that most cannabis today is a hybrid of some kind. Several genetic and chemical studies have found that a strain's label is an unreliable guide to its genetics or chemical makeup. Two strains labeled indica can differ from each other more than an indica differs from a sativa.

Some brands now describe products by their dominant terpenes or by the experience people tend to report, rather than relying on the three classic labels alone.

sections.heading: Why chemistry matters more
sections.html:
How a strain feels seems to depend more on its chemistry than its category. Start with cannabinoids: how much THC and CBD it contains, plus any minor cannabinoids on the label. Our guide to cannabinoids covers the basics.

Then look at terpenes, the aromatic compounds behind a strain's scent, such as earthy myrcene, bright limonene, piney pinene and peppery caryophyllene. Some people find that the terpenes they enjoy are a better guide than any label. Our terpenes guide goes deeper.

Your own body matters too. Tolerance, the amount you take, how you consume and even your setting can all shape the experience. The same strain can even feel different from one day to the next.

sections.heading: Using the labels as a loose guide
sections.html:
None of this makes the labels useless. They are a reasonable shorthand, especially when you are starting out. A few ways to use them well:

  • See the label as a starting point, not a promise.
  • Check the cannabinoid and terpene details alongside it.
  • Follow your nose, since aroma can be a helpful clue.
  • Keep notes on strains you enjoy, and look for patterns in their terpenes.
  • Start low and go slow with anything new.

When you are ready to put this into practice, Uforia's live menu of flower and pre-rolls is a good place to explore, whether you visit us in Jersey City or order delivery.

takeaways: Indica and sativa began as botanical names in the 1700s.
Today the labels loosely describe expected experiences, and most strains are hybrids.
Cannabinoids and terpenes say more about a strain than its category.
Use the labels as a starting point, and start low and go slow.
